newsitem.title: CHILE: Chilean building boom will ebb in 1997 - industry.
newsitem.headline: Chilean building boom will ebb in 1997 - industry.

text.p: Chile's construction boom would probably deflate a bit in 1997, especially if the Central Bank's kept holding the reins on economic growth with high interest rates, the head of the industry's main trade group said.

The construction industry -- one of the most dynamic sectors in Chile's already fast-growing economy -- should see about 7.6 percent growth this year after 10.3 percent growth in 1996 in terms of total investment, said Chilean Construction Chamber President Hernan Doren.
He attributed the drop squarely to "the adjustment," or the Central Bank's tight-credit policies aimed at squeezing the life out of Chile's stubborn inflation.

"This is a consequence of the process of adjustment in the economy...and it's going to start to be felt more in the provinces," he told a news conference, adding that the slowdown has already been felt starting in late 1996, but so far mainly in Santiago.

A building boom in Santiago has left the city center and eastern suburbs bristling with post-Modernist skyscrapers and apartment blocks, some of them architectural prize-winners and others widely disdained as monstrosities.

In November, Compania de Telecomunicaciones de Chile cut the ribbon on the country's tallest building, the 32-story CTC Tower, the company's corporate headquarters. A giant steel-and-glass rectangle with an antenna, Santiaguinos often quip that it looks like a giant cellular phone.
Doren said the 1996 rise was due partly to a 34.7 percent rise in public infrastructure building and the coming drop was already reflected in a decline in building permits issued in Santiago.

Housing construction in Santiago fell 25 percent in the September-to-November quarter, showing the effects of the adjustment, but was offset by a rise of a roughly similar rate in the rest of the country, he said. Complete figures for December were not available yet.
Central Bank President Carlos Massad has said interest rates may be relaxed soon, but any reduction will be gradual, and few analysts expect any move on rates before February or March.
